original_question: Explain the paradox that generic steady three-dimensional Euler fields appear topologically regular while Beltrami fields can realize arbitrarily complicated topology, and determine the natural notion of genericity for steady fields.
target_in_paper: Section 12, Problem 33: "Explain this paradox: what is a typical steady field and what genericity notion is natural for steady fields?" ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's exact open problem unusually well: it identifies the paradox between the topological regularity of generic steady three-dimensional Euler fields and the topological complexity of Beltrami fields, and it asks for the natural notion of genericity for steady fields. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))
missing_details: The steady Euler setting should be stated explicitly: one is considering steady incompressible Euler flows v on a domain M, with v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0, and v tangent to the boundary ∂M. In the paradox itself, the discussion is specifically about 3D steady fields. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

The 'topologically regular' side is not about arbitrary smooth steady fields: it is the case of an analytic steady 3D field that is not everywhere collinear with its curl, for which the domain is almost everywhere fibered into invariant tori and annuli. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

The paper also inserts an intermediate case omitted from your draft: if the steady field is everywhere collinear with its vorticity, but the proportionality coefficient is a generic function, then the domain is still fibered in a similar way. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

The 'chaotic' side should be identified more precisely as the Beltrami case, i.e. fields satisfying curl v = λv, where the paper notes that the topology can be very intricate and then gives nearby examples involving knotted/linked vortex lines and tubes. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

To be fully paper-faithful, the question should ask not just for an explanation of the contrast, but specifically: what should count as a typical steady field, and what genericity notion is natural on the space of steady Euler fields? ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

A hidden contextual detail is that the paper warns that 'typical' in hydrodynamics may differ from standard genericity notions, because stationary 2D stream functions can have analytic level sets despite only finite smoothness across the levels; the nearby detailed discussion of this appears in Section 6.2. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))

No algebraic data such as ambient ring, homogeneity degree, or nilpotency condition are relevant here; the missing stand-alone details are PDE setup, dimension, operator definitions, regularity assumptions, and the exact classes of steady fields being contrasted. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))
refined_question: For steady incompressible Euler flows v on a three-dimensional domain M ⊂ R3, satisfying v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0, and v tangent to ∂M, explain the following paradox from the paper: Arnold's theory says that an analytic steady field that is not everywhere collinear with curl v is almost everywhere fibered by invariant tori and annuli, and that a similar fibration persists when v is everywhere collinear with its vorticity but the proportionality factor is a generic function, whereas Beltrami eigenfields satisfying curl v = λv can realize arbitrarily complicated topology; specifically, what should count as a typical steady field, and what notion of genericity is natural on the space of steady Euler fields? ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))
justification: This is clearly Problem 33 in Section 12, not a broader neighboring issue, because the draft mirrors the exact vocabulary and logical structure of that problem: the surrounding paragraph first contrasts Arnold's almost-everywhere torus/annulus fibration for analytic steady 3D fields with the intricate topology available to Beltrami fields, then immediately asks for the proper notion of a typical steady field and the natural genericity notion. The paper further remarks that hydrodynamic typicality may be nonstandard, and the nearby supporting context for that warning is the discussion of partially analytic stationary 2D stream functions in Section 6.2. ([math.toronto.edu](https://www.math.toronto.edu/khesin/papers/Problems_in_GHD_ARMA.pdf))
